facts.statement: These birds stood over two meters tall and were likely herbivorous.
facts.quote: Over two metres in height, they were likely herbivorous.

facts.statement: Genyornis was the last known member of the extinct family Dromornithidae, which existed in Australia for over 30 million years.
facts.quote: It is the last known member of the extinct flightless bird family Dromornithidae, which had been part of the fauna of the Australian continent for over 30 million years.

facts.statement: The original specimen, a left femur, was found at Lake Callabonna in South Australia.
facts.quote: The specimen is a left femur. It was found at Lake Callabonna in South Australia.

facts.statement: Fossils of Genyornis have been found in articulation, a state not yet discovered in any other dromornithid species.
facts.quote: The fossils of the species have been found remaining in articulation, and no other dromornithid species has been discovered in this state.

facts.statement: Gastroliths (stomach stones) have been found with Genyornis remains, indicating the fossils were often found in shallow sites.
facts.quote: Gastroliths belonging to these animals have been found alongside their remains, a feature that has revealed the sometimes shallow site of fossils.

facts.statement: Recent studies found that Genyornis had a goose-like bill with a raised triangular casque.
facts.quote: Namely, the bill was found to be much more goose-like, with a raised triangular casque.

facts.statement: Genyornis fossils have been found in South Australia and New South Wales dating to the Pleistocene Epoch.
facts.quote: This mihirung has been found at sites in South Australia and New South Wales, dating to the Pleistocene Epoch.

facts.statement: Eggshell fragments from around 200 sites show burn marks, suggesting humans collected and cooked Genyornis eggs.
facts.quote: A 2015 study collected egg shell fragments of Genyornis from around 200 sites that show burn marks.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the eggshells with burn marks belonged to Genyornis or the extinct giant malleefowl.
facts.quote: A later study suggested that the eggs actually belonged to the giant malleefowl, a species of extinct megapode.

facts.statement: A 2022 study using protein sequences concluded the eggshells likely belonged to Genyornis, supporting earlier implications.
facts.quote: A 2022 study examined the protein sequences of these unidentified eggshells and, through phylogenetic analysis, concluded that the lineage that produced these eggs diverged prior to the emergence of megapodes, supporting the previous implication that the eggs in question were produced by Genyornis.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate between human impact and changing climate as the primary causes of Genyornis extinction.
facts.quote: Two main theories propose a cause for megafauna extinction - human impact and changing climate.

facts.statement: Archaeologists found a rock painting possibly 40,000 years old that depicts two Genyornis individuals.
facts.quote: In May 2010, archaeologists announced the rediscovery of an Aboriginal rock art painting, possibly 40,000 years old, at the Nawarla Gabarnmung rock art site in the Northern Territory, that they suggested depicts two Genyornis individuals.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the rock art depicts Genyornis, as some studies suggest the art is only 14,000 years old and indistinguishable from other birds.
facts.quote: A later study suggested that the painting could not be more than 14,000 years old, long after the bird is thought to have gone extinct, and it could not be morphologically distinguished from depictions of other birds.

facts.statement: Genyornis individuals at Lake Callabonna showed signs of osteomyelitis, likely caused by getting stuck in drying mud.
facts.quote: The birds recovered from the site seemed to have been particularly prone to osteomyelitis, as a result of getting stuck in the mud of the drying lake bed as the water receded.

facts.statement: A 2024 study suggests Genyornis had adaptations for feeding on aquatic plants, tying them closely to freshwater habitats.
facts.quote: A 2024 study of the skull morphology of Genyornis found apparent adaptations to feeding on aquatic plants, making them closely tied to freshwater habitats.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Genyornis extinction was caused by their reliance on freshwater habitats that dried up during late Pleistocene aridification.
facts.quote: A reliance on these habitats may have made the species uniquely vulnerable to the loss of freshwater lakes during the aridification of Australia during the late Pleistocene, potentially leading to its extinction.

facts.statement: Genyornis newtoni was a flightless bird that lived in Australia until 50,000 years ago.
facts.quote: Genyornis newtoni es una especie extinta de ave anseriforme no voladora que vivió en Australia hasta hace 50 000 años.

facts.statement: The species stood 2.5 meters tall and weighed between 200 and 240 kilograms.
facts.quote: Medía 2,5 metros de altura y pesaba de 200 a 240 kg.

facts.statement: Its closest living relatives are ducks and geese.
facts.quote: Sus parientes más cercanos son los actuales anímidos, patos y gansos.

facts.statement: The shape of its beak suggests it was a combination of predator and scavenger.
facts.quote: La forma del pico sugiere que eran una combinación de depredadores y carroñeros.

facts.quote: Parent group: Dromornithidae

facts.statement: The genus lived from the Gelasian to the Late Pleistocene, between 2.58 and 0.0117 million years ago.
